## Estimation mechanics

<!-- Moved from ch. 8's "Estimation" subsection. -->

- CUE quadratic objective. The weighting matrix keeps every eigen-direction of $\hat\Omega/n$ with a positive eigenvalue [@AK2020]; $\hat\Omega$ is clustered by plant.
- $\tilde g$ by self-normalized importance sampling: 1,000 fixed draws per firm from a mixture of a uniform and two log-uniform proposals on the support (uniform in $M$, log-uniform in $M$, and log-uniform in the distance to the support's lower edge), reweighted. Fixed draws make the objective smooth in $(\theta,\gamma)$ [@Schennach2014, p. 360].
- Reference measure: @Schennach2014's Proposition 2.1, $\exp(-\|D^{-1}(g(M)-g(M^*))\|^2)$ times the uniform on the support, with the row scales $D$ computed once and held fixed across every compared fit.
- **Gross sales-tax revenue is observed.** The data record the sales tax each firm pays on its sales in each period, which is the observed counterpart of $\tau_{S,it}P_tY_{it}$ in @eq-govt-rev; total revenue in the counterfactual is computed from it directly, held at its baseline value.
- **The score rows enter in bounded form.** With $B=1-(1+\lambda_1)x^{\lambda_1}$, the scores of $h$ are $\partial h/\partial\lambda_1=-x^{\lambda_1}[1+(1+\lambda_1)\ln x]/B$ and $\partial h/\partial\bar\lambda=\lambda_1(1+\lambda_1)x^{\lambda_1}/(\bar\lambda B)$. Both diverge at the FOC ceiling ($B\to0$), where a single extreme draw can dominate the weighting matrix. The rows use the softsign $s/(1+|s|)\in(-1,1)$ instead ($B$ floored at $10^{-6}$); softsign rather than $s/(1-s)$ because the score in $\lambda_1$ changes sign. Validity is unaffected: any function of $e$ alone is independent of $\varepsilon$. The transform decays polynomially, so firms stay distinguishable across the range of $e$; $\exp$ and $\tanh$ saturate.
- Nelder–Mead, two passes; every grid point starts from the same validated point (no chaining across points), with common random numbers within a fit. $\gamma$ is solved for at the start point.
- $\gamma$ is unbounded in the optimizer: @Schennach2014 and @AK2020 both treat $\gamma\to\pm\infty$ as an expected solution, not a numerical failure.
- Implementation of h's socres: $s_{\lambda_1}$ and $s_{\bar\lambda}$ are the scores of $h$ in $\lambda_1$ and $\bar\lambda$, bounded by $s/(1+|s|)$.
- Implementation of $\psi \ind \tau_P$: $\bar\tau_{P,jt}$ is the leave-one-out industry–year mean purchases rate
- For the seventeen moments, the 95 percent critical value is $\chi^2_{17,.95}=27.59$.
- 

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
**Superseded (linear $q$, single-tax run, 2026-09-22).**

- **The $\lambda$-score moment enters in bounded form.** The score $h_\lambda(e)\equiv\partial h(e;\lambda)/\partial\lambda=-2e/(1-2\lambda e)$ diverges near the FOC ceiling $e\to1/(2\lambda)$, where a single extreme draw can dominate the weighting matrix's eigenvalues and silently collapse the effective moment count. The implementation therefore replaces $h_\lambda$ with $h_\lambda/(1-h_\lambda)\in(-1,0]$ in the ninth moment ($1-2\lambda e$ floored at $10^{-6}$). Validity is unaffected: any function of $e$ alone is independent of $\varepsilon$ under the same argument that licenses the raw score. The transform decays polynomially, not exponentially, so firms stay numerically distinguishable across the whole range of $e$; $\exp(h_\lambda)$ and $\tanh(h_\lambda)$ were rejected because both saturate to a constant for most of the sample.
- Per-firm Metropolis chain: $n_{burn}=1000$, $n_{keep}=3000$ [(settled convention -- see CLAUDE.md's "MCMC chain-length convention" entry for why this length, not a longer one, and why acceptance-rate SD is the more reliable diagnostic than $\gamma'g$ variance)]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}.
- Nelder-Mead optimizer [(beats BOBYQA decisively on this problem -- see CLAUDE.md)]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}.
:::

## Trim cutoff

<!-- Moved from ch. 8's "Estimation" subsection, including @fig-cf-trim. -->

- Top 0.5 percent of interior firms by $M^*$ dropped before fitting: 61 firm-years, 22 of them in 321.
- Without the trim, no tested $(\lambda_1,\bar\lambda)$ passes the conservative test (best $TS=46.1$ against 27.59).
- The largest firms in 321 report 7 to 13 times $\bar M_{j,t-1}$. At the operating point, the FOC ceiling caps their overreporting at about $0.24\,\bar M_{j,t-1}$ ($u\lesssim0.02$), against an observed $\mathcal V_{it}\approx0.27$.
- The trimmed firms enter the counterfactual mechanically: their claims scale with the rate.

## Search over the detection parameters $(\lambda_1,\bar\lambda)$

- $(\lambda_1,\bar\lambda)$ is fixed on a grid; at each point $(\delta_0,\delta_1,\delta_2)$ and $\gamma$ are estimated.
- Coarse grid: $\lambda_1\in\{0.65,0.70,0.75\}\times\bar\lambda\in\{0.5,4.5,9\}$. Only $(0.75,0.5)$ passes the conservative test ($TS=23.7$); the next best is $(0.70,9)$ at 29.5.
- Fine grid around it: $\lambda_1\in\{0.725,0.75,0.775\}\times\bar\lambda\in\{0.4,0.5,0.6\}$.
- A second point passes on the fine grid: $(\lambda_1,\bar\lambda)=(0.775,0.5)$, $TS=22.0$ ($R=1000$; 23.8 at $R=4000$, against 23.7 and 24.7 at the operating point), with all 17 directions kept and $(\hat\delta_0,\hat\delta_1,\hat\delta_2)=(42.2,27.1,3.87)$, $\hat\omega^*=3.50$. The difference in $TS$ is within the noise between refits, and the fit is less settled (smaller effective sample size per firm, larger $\gamma$), so the operating point stays at $(0.75,0.5)$; the passing region is not a single point.
- The moments do not pin down the level of detection $\bar\lambda$; relative detection risk is nearly free of it: across industries, relative risk at $\bar\lambda=0.5$ and $\bar\lambda=9$ correlates at 0.87.

## Test inversion: the conservative test, and why

<!-- OUTLINE, not yet prose -- pulled from CLAUDE.md so the numbers/formulas are ready to
write from directly; still your own argument to make. Ch. 8's body keeps its one-line
statement of the test (TS=2n*Lhat against chi2_{d_g,.95}, "conservative" test, what a passing point
means) since results there are unreadable without it -- don't duplicate that here, this
section is the justification for the design, not a restatement of it. -->

- **Source definition (Schennach 2014, Definition F.1 and Theorem F.1):** with $\hat g(\theta,\gamma)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\tilde g(Z_i,\theta,\gamma)$ (the sample average of the tilted moment from @eq-elvis-tilt) and $\hat V(\theta,\gamma)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\tilde g(Z_i,\theta,\gamma)\tilde g(Z_i,\theta,\gamma)'$, her continuous updating objective is $\hat L_n^S(\theta)=\sup_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{d_g}}-\tfrac12\,\hat g(\theta,\gamma)'\hat V(\theta,\gamma)^{-}\hat g(\theta,\gamma)$, with $\hat V^-$ a generalized inverse. Theorem F.1: at any $\theta$ satisfying the moment condition, $-2n\hat L_n^S(\theta)$ is asymptotically bounded above by $\chi^2_{d_g}$. Maximizing $\hat L_n^S$ over $\gamma$ is the same as minimizing the nonnegative quadratic form $\tfrac12\hat g'\hat V^-\hat g$; we report this positive quantity as $\hat L_n(\theta)$, so $TS(\theta)=2n\hat L_n(\theta)=-2n\hat L_n^S(\theta)$ — same statistic, sign flipped purely so the optimizer minimizes a nonnegative objective instead of maximizing a nonpositive one. $\hat V^-$ in our implementation keeps every eigen-direction with a positive eigenvalue, following @AK2020.
- **Conservative test** (Theorem F.1, absolute): $TS_{\text{cons}}=2n\hat L_n$ against $\chi^2_{d_g,.95}$ directly -- no credit for profiling out nuisance parameters or $\gamma$.
- **Why the conservative test:** the counterfactual's purpose is to support a policy claim, so the confidence sets use the test whose size is guaranteed not to exceed its nominal level.

<!-- DROPPED 2026-09-23 (Hans): the soft (min-subtracted) test is not used in the thesis.
- **Two test statistics, same $\hat L_n$, different critical value:**
  - **Conservative test** (Theorem F.1, absolute): $TS_{\text{cons}}=2n\hat L_n$ against $\chi^2_{d_g,.95}$ directly -- no credit for profiling out nuisance parameters or $\gamma$.
  - **Soft test** (min-subtracted, CHT-style): $TS_{\text{soft}}=2n[\hat L_n-\min\hat L_n]$ against the same $\chi^2_{d_g,.95}$ -- profiling gives back some degrees of freedom informally, so this is strictly more powerful (rejects more), and $TS_{\text{cons}}=TS_{\text{soft}}+2n\hat L_{n,\min}$ exactly, a fixed additive shift. The conservative-passing region is therefore always nested inside the soft-passing region.
- **Why the conservative test is reported as headline here** (a real, considered choice, not the only one used in this project -- the stage-2 $(\lambda,\delta_1,\delta_2)$ estimates elsewhere use the soft test as operative): once genuine conservative-test-passing points existed for the first time in this project's history (the 3D cube result, @sec-cf-estimates), the more conservative test became the defensible one to lead with for a counterfactual whose whole purpose is to make a policy claim -- the soft test remains reported alongside it, not discarded.
-->

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- **Why test inversion over a bootstrap CI:** an earlier attempt (plant-block bootstrap on the PF-step elasticities, a different part of this project) gave bias-corrected percentile intervals that crossed outside the parameter's own natural domain ($[0,1]$ for an elasticity) -- an artifact of the CI formula, not of the estimator. Test inversion only ever evaluates points on the bounded grid actually tested, so this can't happen; the "cost" is a set-valued answer instead of a point $\pm$ SE, treated in this project as an honest feature, not a fallback (Schennach herself: adding moments shrinks the identified set, "not a fallback to avoid").
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- **Precedent in @AK2020, followed directly, not just cited:** their own counterfactual appendix (`Appendix_F/F_figure1.R`) uses exactly this design -- grid a candidate outcome, profile the nuisance parameters (their $\gamma$) at each cell, plot pass/fail by candidate, connect the passing region's own upper/lower bounds across the grid. The bound-plot convention used for every $(\Delta,R)$ figure in this chapter (grey $\times$ = rejected, coloured $\bullet$ = passes, dashed/dotted bound lines) is a direct visual analogue of their own figure, not an independent design.
:::

## Counterfactual implementation {#sec-app-cf-implementation}

This section states every formula the counterfactual computes, for one firm-year $i$ and one candidate value $M$ of its true materials. Materials are measured as real expenditure (nominal expenditure divided by $p_{\text{gdp}}$), so purchase credits are $\tau_{P,it}M$. The counterfactual purchases rate is $\tilde\tau_{P,it}=(1+\Delta)\tau_{P,it}$; the rate on sales $\tau_{S,it}$ does not change.

**Held fixed.** The detection and cost parameters at the operating point, including the detection scale $\lambda_{0,jt}=1/(\bar\lambda\bar M_{j,t-1})$: it is a parameter of the detection function, set through the industry's lagged mean of reported materials, so it does not move with the firm's current choices; capital and labour; productivity $\omega_{it}$, the cost shock $\psi_{it}$ and the output measurement error $\varepsilon_{it}$; and prices $P_t$, $\rho_t$.

### Baseline objects at a candidate $M$

From the data $Z_{it}$ and a candidate $M\in\big(\max\{0,M^*_{it}-c_{\lambda_1}/\lambda_{0,jt}\},M^*_{it}\big)$:
$$
e=M^*_{it}-M,\qquad x=\lambda_{0,jt}\,e,\qquad B\equiv1-(1+\lambda_1)x^{\lambda_1}.
$$
The baseline evasion FOC, $\tau_{P,it}\rho_t\big(1-(1+\lambda_1)x^{\lambda_1}\big)=\exp\{\delta_0-\delta_1\omega+\delta_2\omega^2+\psi\}$, says that $B$ is the firm's marginal cost of evasion relative to its marginal benefit, $B=\exp\{\delta_0-\delta_1\omega+\delta_2\omega^2+\psi\}/(\tau_{P,it}\rho_t)$. Each candidate $M$ therefore pins down the firm's type $(\omega,\psi)$, and the tilt integrates over candidates.

### New evasion

At the new rate, the same marginal cost (same $\omega$, $\psi$, linear cost in $e$) meets a marginal benefit scaled by $1+\Delta$:
$$
(1+\Delta)\tau_{P,it}\rho_t\big(1-(1+\lambda_1)x'^{\lambda_1}\big)=\tau_{P,it}\rho_t B
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x'^{\lambda_1}=\max\Big\{0,\ \frac{1-B/(1+\Delta)}{1+\lambda_1}\Big\},\qquad e'=x'/\lambda_{0,jt}.
$$ {#eq-app-cf-eprime}

Since $B/(1+\Delta)>0$, $x'^{\lambda_1}<1/(1+\lambda_1)$: the new evasion stays below the FOC ceiling $c_{\lambda_1}$ for any $\Delta$. A firm with $B\ge1+\Delta$ stops overreporting.

**Why $e'$ does not depend on the response of $M$.** The evasion FOC contains $\tau_{P,it}\rho_t$, the detection probability $q(e)$ through $\lambda_{0,jt}$ and $\lambda_1$, and the marginal cost $\exp\{\delta_0-\delta_1\omega+\delta_2\omega^2+\psi\}$. None of these is $M$: the detection parameter $\lambda_{0,jt}$ does not depend on the firm's materials, and the cost depends on productivity, not on the input level. So when $M$ re-optimizes, the evasion FOC is unchanged and @eq-app-cf-eprime holds as is. The candidate $M$ enters $e'$ only through the baseline $B$, as the firm's type. (Symmetrically, the materials FOC below contains no $e$: $M\perp e\mid\omega$.)

### Response of true materials

The materials FOC with the two rates (@sec-model) is, with true output $Y=K^{\alpha_K}L^{\alpha_L}M^{\beta}\exp(\omega)$,
$$
(1-\tau_{S,it})P_t\,\beta K^{\alpha_K}L^{\alpha_L}M^{\beta-1}\exp(\omega)=(1-\tau_{P,it})\rho_t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
M=\left[\frac{(1-\tau_{S,it})P_t\beta K^{\alpha_K}L^{\alpha_L}\exp(\omega)}{(1-\tau_{P,it})\rho_t}\right]^{\frac1{1-\beta}}.
$$
Taking the ratio of this solution at $\tilde\tau_{P,it}$ and at $\tau_{P,it}$, everything except the purchases rate cancels:
$$
r_{it}(\Delta)\equiv\frac{M(\Delta)}{M}=\left(\frac{1-(1+\Delta)\tau_{P,it}}{1-\tau_{P,it}}\right)^{-\frac1{1-\beta}}.
$$ {#eq-app-cf-r}

**Why $r$ does not depend on $M$.** The level of $M$ is set by $K$, $L$, $\omega$, $P_t$, $\rho_t$ and $\tau_{S,it}$, all held fixed, so they cancel in the ratio. The ratio depends only on $\tau_{P,it}$, $\Delta$ and $\beta$. It is therefore the same for every candidate $M$ of a firm: whatever the firm's true materials are, they scale by the same factor. With $\beta\approx0.39$ and $\tau_P\approx0.088$, the elasticity of $M$ with respect to the purchases rate at $\Delta=0$ is $\tau_P/[(1-\beta)(1-\tau_P)]\approx0.16$. The new true materials are $M'=r_{it}(\Delta)M$, and reported materials become $M'+e'$.

Output and gross sales-tax revenue scale with $M^{\beta}$, holding $K$, $L$, $\omega$ and the measurement error $\varepsilon$ fixed: $Y'=r_{it}^{\beta}Y$, so observed gross sales-tax revenue becomes $t1_{it}\,r_{it}^{\beta}$, where $t1_{it}=\tau_{S,it}\times$ nominal reported sales.

### Claimed deductions and revenue

Claims are the credit on true purchases plus the credit on undetected overreporting:
$$
C_i(\Delta;M)=(1+\Delta)\tau_{P,it}\Big[r_{it}(\Delta)\,M+\big(1-q(e')\big)e'\Big],\qquad q(e')=x'^{\lambda_1},
$$ {#eq-app-cf-claims}
and net sales-tax revenue from the firm, in real terms, is
$$
R_i(\Delta;M)=\frac{t1_{it}\,r_{it}(\Delta)^{\beta}}{p_{\text{gdp},t}}-C_i(\Delta;M).
$$ {#eq-app-cf-revenue}
With true materials held fixed (the robustness version), $r_{it}\equiv1$: claims use $M$ and the sales tax is the observed $t1_{it}/p_{\text{gdp},t}$.

### Estimation

The target is the expected value per firm-year, in units of $S=n^{-1}\sum_i\tau_{P,it}M^*_{it}$ (the mean claimed credit in the data), entered as one more moment with its own parameter $T$:
$$
g_{10}(M,Z_{it};T)=\frac{R_i(\Delta;M)}{S}-T .
$$
Only $\gamma$ is free; $\theta$ stays at the operating point [@AK2020, App. F]. For each firm the tilted moment is the importance-sampling average over draws $M^{(s)}$ of the latent,
$$
\tilde g_{10,i}=\sum_s w_{is}(\gamma)\,g_{10}(M^{(s)},Z_{it};T),\qquad w_{is}(\gamma)=\frac{\pi_{is}\exp\big(\gamma'g(M^{(s)},Z_{it})\big)}{\sum_{s'}\pi_{is'}\exp\big(\gamma'g(M^{(s')},Z_{it})\big)},
$$
where $\pi_{is}$ is the importance weight of draw $s$ with respect to the reference density $f^0_{M|Z}$ and $g$ includes $g_{10}$. The draws are the same for every $T$ and $\Delta$. The sales-tax term $t1_{it}r_{it}^{\beta}/(p_{\text{gdp},t}S)$ is the same for every draw of firm $i$: it cancels in the weights and adds a firm-level constant to $\tilde g_{10,i}$. It still enters the variance $\hat\Omega$ across firms. The moment is linear in $T$, so the profiled statistic is
$$
TS(T)=2n\min_{\gamma}\hat L_n(\hat\theta,\gamma;T),
$$
$\hat T$ is its minimizer, and the reported set is the conservative one, $\{T:TS(T)\le\chi^2_{d_g,.95}\}$ with $d_g=18$ (the 17 estimation rows plus row 10). Row 10 is left out of the reference measure's penalty, since it is bounded for each firm. Because a failed inner solve can only raise $TS$, each $\gamma$ problem is solved from several starting values (the operating $\gamma$, the solution at the previous $T$, and the best solution found so far), keeping the lowest; the set is the union of every $T$ accepted along the way, located by bisection outward from $\hat T$. Revenue per firm-year is $\hat T\times S$, and the set's bounds scale the same way.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- **What this is:** one forward-simulation run at the already-fixed headline $(\hat\theta,\hat\gamma)$, $\Delta=0$ (current policy), across all 32,232 trimmed lag_m firm-periods -- no fitting, just evaluating each firm's posterior-mean evasion and revenue at the point already estimated in @sec-cf-estimates. Confirms internal consistency on its own: mean $R_{\text{real}}=\$1702.24$, sitting exactly inside the baseline $[1666,1745]$ CI of the (dropped) CV-adjusted revenue results.
:::

**Revenue lost to undetected evasion:**

- Mean $\text{Loss}_i=\tau_{P,i}(1-q(e_i))e_i$ (the extra credit paid out that perfect detection would have caught) across all firms: **\$53.32 real COP per firm-period**; **\$1,718,598** total across the sample.
- **Reported as a share of *potential* revenue, the standard VAT-gap convention** -- not of actual collections. Potential $=$ actual $+$ loss $=1702.24+53.32=\$1755.56$; gap $=1-\text{actual/potential}=\textbf{3.04\%}$. [Verified this is the right denominator directly against the methodology already read for @sec-cf-question's country comparisons: the EU VAT Gap Report's own VTTL/"percent of VTTL" construction and CIAT's Efficiency$=$actual/potential decomposition both divide by potential, never by actual.]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- **A narrow-channel number[, say so explicitly]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}:** one mechanism (materials-credit overreporting), one country, one structural sample -- smaller than the official comparators' *non-compliance-only* gap shares (14.1 percent Colombia, 30.7 percent Chile, 54.4 percent Mexico, all CIAT, as % of potential), which capture every form of non-compliance, not just this channel. [Smaller than that broader base is the expected, reassuring result: not implausibly large (like the disqualified Poland claim), not zero either.]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

**Revenue elasticity of the tax rate:**

- Closed form[, derived by hand]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"} from the same $\tilde e(\Delta)$ used throughout this chapter: $\dfrac{\partial R_i}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=1}=-\tau_{P,i}\left[M_i-e_i+\lambda e_i^2+\dfrac{1}{2\lambda}\right]$, $x\equiv1+\Delta$.
- **Two one-sided elasticities, not one** -- the same kink at $\Delta=0$ documented in @sec-cf-results makes the two-sided derivative ill-defined: $\varepsilon_{\text{right}}=-20.30$, $\varepsilon_{\text{left}}=-9.68$ (both aggregate, ratio of means, $x=1$). Both large; the asymmetry is the same mechanism as the Results section's own asymmetric-response finding, not a new one.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- Cross-validated: the closed form's aggregate mean ($-34{,}575.96$ real COP) agrees with the numerical right-derivative ($-34{,}559.47$, from tiny $\Delta=\pm0.001$ runs) to **0.048 percent**.
:::

- **Elasticity "with respect to the tax rate" is the same number, not a third one, and this is exact, not approximate.** The model only ever moves $\tau_P$ through the proportional shifter $x$ ($\tilde\tau_{P,i}=x\tau_{P,i}$, $\tau_{P,i}$ fixed), so $d\ln\tilde\tau_{P,i}=d\ln x$ identically at every firm, every $x$ -- not just at $\Delta=0$. [Confirmed a second, independent way: $\tau_{P,i}$ cancels out of $\tilde e_i(\Delta)$ entirely in the FOC derivation, so a firm's own rate level doesn't even affect how its evasion responds to a proportional shock. A genuinely different "elasticity to an absolute percentage-point change" would need its own derivation (a non-proportional shock design) -- not computed here, flagged only.]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
- Median interior-firm elasticity, as a distinct "typical firm" measure: $-195.99$ -- far larger in magnitude because the median evading firm's own $R_i$ is much smaller than the sample mean [(a real heterogeneity finding, not a discrepancy with the aggregate number above)]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}.
:::
